title: King Henry Walks Among His Soldiers
text:
In Shakespeare's Henry V, the English army lies outnumbered and exhausted on the night before the battle of Agincourt. The king borrows a cloak from old Sir Thomas Erpingham and walks through the camp in disguise.

He falls into conversation with three common soldiers, John Bates, Alexander Court and Michael Williams. Bates says the king may be brave, but he would rather be up to his neck in the Thames than here. Henry, posing as an ordinary soldier, says he would die happily in the king's company, since his cause is just. Williams answers that this is more than they know. And if the cause is not good, the king himself has a heavy reckoning to make, when all the legs and arms and heads chopped off in battle join together at the last day and cry out.

Henry argues that each soldier's soul is his own, and the king is not responsible for every man's sins. But the words strike home. Henry and Williams quarrel and exchange gloves, promising to settle it after the battle.

Alone, Henry speaks of the burden of kingship: everything is laid on the king. What does he have that ordinary men lack, except ceremony? He envies the peasant who sleeps soundly. After the victory, he reveals himself to Williams and has his glove filled with crowns.
lesson: Listening to the people you lead, without your title in the room, tells you what reports never will. Take what you hear seriously, including the hard part about your responsibility for them.
people: Henry V, Michael Williams, John Bates, Alexander Court, Sir Thomas Erpingham
source: William Shakespeare, Henry V, Act 4, Scene 1 and Scene 8
